choices.feedback: Exactly right. You stayed in scope, gave her a real timeline, and delegated the fall risk instead of dropping it. Now actually tell the nurse.

choices.text: 'Your CT looked okay from what I saw on the board.'
choices.feedback: Out of scope and possibly wrong. Even a correct guess relayed by a tech is a serious problem. Never interpret results.

choices.text: Say nothing and keep walking; you will come back to both.
choices.feedback: The EKG gets done but you have created an angry patient and left an urgent bathroom request unassigned. Five seconds of speech would have covered both.

choices.text: 'Sorry, I'm busy right now.'
choices.feedback: True and useless. It gives her no path to an answer, which is exactly what turns a reasonable person into a complaint.

steps.prompt: You are in room 11. The patient is a 64-year-old man, diaphoretic, holding his fist against his sternum. The EKG is acquired at 1424.

choices.text: Carry the tracing directly to the nearest attending or APP and hand it to them
choices.feedback: Correct. The metric is not acquisition, it is provider review. Put it in a hand and get the review time documented.

choices.text: Leave the tracing on the EKG machine and tell the nurse it is done
choices.feedback: An unreviewed tracing is a tracing nobody has acted on. The clock keeps running while it sits on the cart.

choices.text: Place the tracing in the chart rack outside the room and document that the EKG is complete
choices.feedback: Documentation is right, placement is wrong. For a possible STEMI the tracing goes into a provider's hands, not a rack.

choices.text: Look at it yourself first to see whether it seems urgent enough to interrupt anyone
choices.feedback: You are not the filter. Techs should learn to recognize an alarming tracing so they walk faster, never to decide whether a provider needs to see one.

steps.prompt: The attending reads it at 1425, says 'that's not a STEMI, but keep him on the monitor,' and moves on. You now have three tasks left: room 12's blood draw, room 9's turnover, and confirming room 14 got to the bathroom.

choices.text: Confirm room 14 was taken, then draw room 12, then turn over room 9
choices.feedback: Good ordering. The delegated task is verified rather than assumed, the pending lab order restarts a results clock, and the turnover, which affects flow but not a patient in the building, comes last.

choices.text: Turn over room 9 first since EVS is waiting on you
choices.feedback: You optimized for the person who asked loudest. The turnover is genuinely the least time-critical item on the list.

choices.text: Draw room 12 first, then room 9, and assume room 14 was handled
choices.feedback: Never assume a delegated safety task was completed. A patient with an urgent bathroom need and no help is a fall waiting to happen.

choices.text: Take a minute at the desk to chart the EKG before anything else
choices.feedback: Charting the EKG with the correct acquisition and review times does matter, but it is a two-minute task you can batch. Verify the patient safety item first.

steps.prompt: It is 1448. Everything on the original list is done. The nurse for room 8 is at the desk. What is the last thing you owe from this sequence?

choices.text: Tell her that room 8 is asking about her CT, and that you told her the nurse would come speak with her
choices.feedback: This is loop closure. A promise you made on the department's behalf is not complete until the person who can keep it knows about it.

choices.text: Nothing; room 8 will ask again if she still wants to know
choices.feedback: You made a commitment. Making the patient chase it undoes the goodwill you bought with the original sentence.

choices.text: Go back to room 8 and tell her the nurse is busy but will come eventually
choices.feedback: Better than nothing, but you are still the only person carrying the request. It needs to reach someone who can actually answer it.

choices.text: Document your EKG times and task completions, and tell the nurse about room 8
choices.feedback: Best of both. Accurate timestamps and a closed loop. This is what a complete sequence looks like.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern here is triage applied to your own task list. Sort by how fast each task can hurt someone: a possible STEMI in minutes, a fall risk in minutes but delegable, a pending lab order in tens of minutes, a room turnover in flow terms only, and an out-of-scope question in seconds of speech.

Three habits carried this scenario. First, the highest-acuity task goes first even when it is not the loudest request. Second, five seconds of honest speech buys enormous patience from patients and prevents complaints, as long as you stay in scope and never interpret a result. Third, delegated tasks are verified, not assumed, and promises you make are closed with the person who can actually keep them.

Notice what you did not do: you did not interpret a CT, you did not decide whether an EKG was urgent enough to show someone, and you did not let the person physically closest to you set your priorities.

scenarios.title: Four minutes out
scenarios.intro:
0247 on a night shift. The department has eight patients and two boarders. You are mid-task in room 6, replacing a saturated dressing setup for a provider who is coming back to look at a laceration in a few minutes.

The EMS radio crackles at the charge desk. The charge nurse turns and calls across the department: 'Full arrest, four minutes out. Sixties, male, witnessed, bystander CPR, they've got a King airway and two rounds of epi in. Resus one.'

You are the only tech in the department right now. The other tech is on a mandated break off the floor.

steps.prompt: Four minutes. You are holding a half-finished dressing setup in room 6. What do you do first?

choices.text: Finish the dressing setup properly; it will only take two more minutes
choices.feedback: Wrong trade. A laceration setup can wait fifteen minutes; a cardiac arrest cannot wait fifteen seconds. Set it down and go.

choices.text: Set the supplies down, tell the provider the setup is paused for an incoming arrest, and go to resus one
choices.feedback: Correct. You abandoned a low-acuity task and, importantly, you told someone you were abandoning it so it does not silently disappear.

choices.text: Walk to resus one without saying anything to anyone
choices.feedback: Right destination, incomplete communication. The provider returns to a half-built setup and no explanation. One sentence prevents that.

choices.text: Ask the charge nurse whether you are needed for the arrest
choices.feedback: You are the only tech in the department during a cardiac arrest. You are needed. Asking burns part of your four minutes.

steps.prompt: You are in resus one. About three minutes remain. The bay was restocked at the start of the shift. What do you set up?

choices.text: Defibrillator on and pads out of the package, backboard ready, suction on and tested, IV or IO setup out, and the mechanical compression device if your department has one
choices.feedback: This is the list. Everything that costs seconds during the code gets those seconds spent now, before the patient arrives.

choices.text: Pull the crash cart to the bedside and wait for instructions
choices.feedback: The cart is necessary but insufficient. Waiting for instructions in the three minutes you own is three minutes wasted.

choices.text: Set up a full suture tray and warm blankets
choices.feedback: Warming matters after return of circulation, but a suture tray is the wrong equipment for an arrest and takes up the bedside surface you need.

choices.text: Draw up epinephrine so it is ready when they arrive
choices.feedback: Absolutely not. Drawing up a medication is outside your scope in every hospital. Pharmacy or nursing prepares drugs.

steps.prompt: The stretcher comes through the bay doors. A paramedic is on the rails doing compressions. The count of one, two, three moves the patient onto the ED bed, and compressions pause for the transfer.

choices.text: Take over compressions immediately as soon as the patient is on the bed
choices.feedback: Correct, and it is the single highest-value thing you do in a code. Every second without compressions is coronary and cerebral perfusion lost.

choices.text: Attach the monitor leads first, then start compressions
choices.feedback: Leads matter, but never at the cost of compression time. Someone else places leads while compressions continue. Compressions come first.

choices.text: Stand back and wait for the physician to assign roles
choices.feedback: In a well-run code roles get called, but nobody should ever have to ask for compressions to be started. Step in.

choices.text: Ask the paramedic for the full report before anyone touches the patient
choices.feedback: The report is given while the work continues, not instead of it. Pausing care for a handoff narrative is a real and dangerous habit.

steps.prompt: You are compressing. About two minutes in, your shoulders are burning and you notice your depth slipping. The team is focused on the airway and the rhythm check is coming up.

choices.text: Say out loud 'I need a switch at the next rhythm check' and keep full-depth compressions until then
choices.feedback: Exactly right. Announced, planned switches at the rhythm check keep interruptions to a few seconds and keep quality high.

choices.text: Push through the next four minutes; asking to switch looks weak
choices.feedback: Compression quality measurably declines after about two minutes regardless of fitness. Silent fatigue is a shallow-compression problem, not a toughness test.

choices.text: Stop compressions now and step away to find a replacement
choices.feedback: Right need, wrong execution. Never stop until someone has hands ready to take over. Announce and hand off at the rhythm check.

choices.text: Slow the rate slightly to conserve energy until the rhythm check
choices.feedback: Rate and depth both matter and trading one away undoes the perfusion you are generating. Ask for the switch instead.

steps.prompt: At 0312 the physician calls it. The room falls quiet. The family is in the consultation room and social work is on the way. There are still eight other patients in the department, and a half-finished dressing setup in room 6.

choices.text: Restock and clean resus one before doing anything else, then return to room 6 and tell the provider you are ready
choices.feedback: The bay must be ready for the next arrival regardless of how this one ended. Then close the loop on the task you abandoned.

choices.text: Go straight back to room 6; the resus bay can be restocked later in the shift
choices.feedback: This is the exact reasoning that leaves a missing blade or an empty suction canister for the next arrest. Resus is restocked before anything else.

choices.text: Take five minutes outside first, then restock the bay
choices.feedback: The instinct is human and a real need, but the bay comes first because it is a patient safety state. Take the five minutes, and the debrief, after the room is ready.

choices.text: Ask whether a debrief is happening, then restock the bay
choices.feedback: Both matter and the order here is acceptable, since asking takes seconds. Just make sure the restocking actually happens.

scenarios.debrief:
A code coming in reorders the department instantly, and the tech's part is almost entirely preparation and compressions.

The preparation window is the three minutes before arrival, and it is the most useful three minutes you will spend: defibrillator on with pads out, suction on and tested, backboard ready, IV and IO supplies out, compression device staged. Everything you open now is a second you do not lose later. What you never do, in any hospital, is draw up a medication.

On arrival, compressions are the job, and the quality rules are not negotiable: `100-120` per minute, at least `2 inches` deep, full recoil, and an announced switch every 2 minutes at the rhythm check so interruptions stay under about 10 seconds. Announcing fatigue is a quality behavior, not a weakness.

Afterward, two things happen in order. The resuscitation bay is returned to a ready state before anything else, because the next arrest does not care about this one. Then the tasks you abandoned get closed, out loud, with the people who were waiting on them.
